Lauren Fernandes noticed menus and flyers all over with the same sterile look, and thought: what if she could help out small businesses which can't afford creative work, usually?

"He's a local lad here from Carpenterstown, he's a local schoolteacher," said Fine Gael Councillor Ted Leddy, who proposed the motion. "A mural or something like that would be very appropriate."

It would use extra heat from the Poolbeg rubbish incinerator to warm water and send it through pipes underground, into buildings in the city, to keep homes and offices cosy without burning additional fossil fuels.

The projected cost of the council's planned Dublin District Heating Project has risen to more than €130 million, according to a new report from the Local Government Audit Service.

That's a 69 percent increase over what Dublin City Council said about the project in 2022, when it was projecting the total cost at €76.9 million in its capital programme – its multi-annual budget for big one-off projects like this.

The project would use extra heat from the Poolbeg rubbish incinerator to warm water and send it through pipes underground, into buildings in the city, to keep homes and offices cosy without burning additional fossil fuels.

It's one of several district heating projects planned in Ireland, as the government pushes to reduce the amount of fossil fuels used to heat buildings in the country, to help blunt the impacts of climate change.

"This project will be the largest district heating network in the country and contribute significantly to the reduction of CO2," according to the council's most recent capital programme.

Even as this flagship district heating project's budget keeps rising, its timeline keeps stretching out too.

In 2022, the council said the project "has been beset by delays. We now expect to go to the market in early 2023 with construction starting in early 2024. The full project will be rolled out over a 4-year period 2023 to 2026."

Four years later, this new audit report – which was on the agenda for Monday's monthly meeting of the council – says that the "interim phase" of the project "is now forecast to be operational by Q4 2028, with an updated budget of €10.7m".

And "The overall Phase 2 project has an estimated total cost of circa €120m and a revised delivery timeline of 2032", it says.

Although there have been delays, the project is progressing, it seems. The council applied to itself for planning permission on 9 September, and a slew of documents on the details of the massive project are now available for comment until 21 October.

The documents suggest that, as the council has previously said, the project would not initially pipe heat into the homes in the residential neighbourhood of Ringsend, nearest the incinerator on the Poolbeg Peninsula.

Instead, the works would connect to the new Glass Bottle development, dig temporary trenches through Ringsend Park to lay insulated pipes to carry the heat to the high-end apartment and office buildings around Grand Canal Dock, where some tech companies are clustered, and then cross the Liffey to the shiny high-rises of Spencer Dock.

That plan to bypass Ringsend and Irishtown in the initial phases might be in flux though. After initial dismay among some residents there, council officials said in August that they'd look at connecting community facilities in those areas early on.

The Poolbeg incinerator burns rubbish, and that heat boils water, producing steam that runs a thermal turbine generator to produce electricity that's exported to the grid. That's happening already.
